title: Capacity Stitching Sprint: Roadmap & OKR Alignment for Dedicated Autoscale
creator: Maya Chen
description: Quarterly planning ticket to formalize a focused sprint that 'stitches' reserved dedicated pools, predictive warm strategies, and autoscale corridors into a single roadmap slice tied to OKRs. Goal is to reduce tail latency and unit cost for committed customers while enabling safer burst behavior for transient demand.
background: Dedicated customers have reported inconsistent latency during cross-region surges and ops has observed inefficient over-provisioning on short-lived spikes. Prior work introduced warm-pools and predictive prewarm heuristics, but we lack a unified cadence and guardrails that tie those features to SLAs and fiscal guardrails. This sprint aims to consolidate tactics into a repeatable quarterly playbook.
goals: Ship a documented 'Capacity Stitch' playbook that maps traffic profiles to reserve + burst policies
Define OKR-linked metrics: committed SLO attainment, cost-per-1k-requests, effective burst success rate
Create runbook templates for canarying autoscale corridor changes with fallbacks
Deliver a pilot canary (1 customer) for adaptive prewarm signals into Dedicated pools
okrs: OKR-2026-Dedicated-1: Improve committed SLO attainment from 97% to 99% for p99 latency
OKR-2026-Cost-3: Reduce average token cost for reserved workloads by 12% without increasing p99 latency
OKR-2026-Runtime-2: Validate autoscale corridor canary across 3 regions with <5% customer-impact incidents
milestones: 2026-02-23: Delivery of measurement spec and target thresholds
2026-03-05: Engineering spike complete (predictive prewarm + telemetry hook)
2026-03-12: Internal canary with synthetic traffic and cost modeling
2026-03-20: Pilot rollout to one committed customer; collect 2 weeks of signals
scope_in: Policy definitions for reserve + burst stitching
Telemetry hooks for prewarm/prefix cache hits and autoscale trigger reasons
Runbook and canary criteria for rolling corridor changes
Cost modeling templates for capacity-sku tradeoffs
scope_out: Overhaul of billing UI or pricing SKUs
Large-scale cross-tenant rebalancing experiments in this sprint (deferred)
decisions: Adopt a three-layer capacity model: reserve (committed), buffer (short-lived warm-backed), and surge (ephemeral on-demand)
Trigger thresholds set initially to 95th percentile observed QPS over 5m windows for buffer allocation
Pilot uses single-region routing to minimize cross-region variability
tradeoffs: Aggressive prewarm reduces cold-start latency but increases short-term cost — mitigation via buffer timeouts and traffic-weighted heuristics
Canarying only with one customer limits generalizability but reduces blast radius
Tighter SLOs may require higher committed capacity, impacting near-term revenue; we prioritize top-tier enterprise customers for pilot
acceptance_criteria: Playbook doc published in Confluence with step-by-step checklist
Measurement spec wired into Console; metrics visible on a dashboard
Canary run shows <3% request-level errors attributable to policy changes and meets latency targets
Cost model demonstrates projected <=12% unit cost improvement for the pilot workload
